papers.title: Dually tunable YBCO coplanar waveguide resonators based on helium-ion-generated Josephson inductances
papers.abstract: Superconducting microwave circuits with and without Josephson inductances are the Swiss Army knife for many experiments and technologies from quantum information science to astrophysical particle detectors. Despite a large variety of existing circuit types, thin film materials and Josephson junction technologies, a flexible and reliable platform for high-magnetic-field and high-temperature applications is yet to be found. In this manuscript, we investigate coplanar waveguide cavities made of the high-temperature cuprate superconductor YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$ (YBCO), integrated with Josephson inductances and quantum interferometers that are generated by the controlled local irradiation of the YBCO with a focused helium ion beam. We obtain strongly flux-tunable microwave resonators, which not only display periodic interferometer oscillations of resonance frequency and decay rate, but also a superimposed Fraunhofer-like modulation pattern. The latter originates from the magnetic field tuning of the individual Josephson junction critical currents due to the out-of-plane junction barriers. It allows adjusting resonance frequency and flux responsivity independently of each other, potentially enabling tunable microwave circuits with low sensitivity to external magnetic-field noise over a broad range of frequencies. Finally, we investigate the temperature dependence of the cavities, show that they have promising characteristics up to 14$\,$K, and present a model for the junction-induced cavity losses.

summary.summary: YBCO coplanar waveguide cavities integrated with helium-ion-generated Josephson junctions exhibit GHz-range flux tunability via periodic SQUID oscillations overlaid with Fraunhofer-like single-junction modulation due to out-of-plane junction barriers. The devices operate up to 14 K with junction-induced quality factors of $Q_{J0} \sim 200$–$700$, enabling independent tuning of resonance frequency and flux responsivity.
summary.motivation: High-temperature superconductors like YBCO can operate in elevated temperatures and large magnetic fields inaccessible to aluminum, but integrating tunable Josephson inductances has proven difficult; helium-ion-generated barrier junctions offer flexible dose-dependent control of critical currents ($I_c$ varied over three orders of magnitude via line dose $D_\ell$).
summary.method: Three quarter-wave CPW cavities on 50 nm M-type YBCO/MgO were patterned, pre-characterized at 4.2 K to obtain $Q_{\mathrm{int},c} \sim 3000$, then integrated with He-FIB SQUIDs by irradiating at $D_{\mathrm{cav}} = 1100$ ions/nm to create critical currents $I_0 \sim 1.5$–$2.8$ µA; resonance and loss factors were extracted from $S_{21}$ measurements versus bias flux and temperature (2.1–14 K).
summary.result: Cavity R1 showed tuning range $\gtrsim 310$ MHz with $\partial\omega_0/\partial\Phi_b \approx 2\pi \times 5$ GHz$\,\Phi_0^{-1}$, R3 reached $\gtrsim 1$ GHz with $\partial\omega_0/\partial\Phi_b \approx 2\pi \times 24$ GHz$\,\Phi_0^{-1}$; Fraunhofer envelope appeared at $\pm 53\,\Phi_0$ (0.53 mT) allowing frequency tuning at flux sweetspots with zero first-order field noise sensitivity; junction resistance extracted as $R_J \approx 100$ Ω matches dc voltage-state values, enabling loss prediction via $1/Q_{J0} \propto I_0^{-2}$.

papers.title: Fast coherent control of a charge qubit on solid neon with a spin-qubit-compatible resonator
papers.abstract: Electrons floating in vacuum provide a clean platform for quantum information processing owing to their isolation from material defects. In particular, electrons on solid neon have emerged as a promising qubit platform because of their potentially long coherence times. Here, toward spin-qubit realization, we couple a single electron on solid neon to a magnetic-field-compatible superconducting NbTiN nanowire resonator. We realize a charge qubit and demonstrate microwave readout and coherent control, with Rabi frequencies up to 76 MHz, an order of magnitude larger than in previous studies. Under strong driving, we observe a qubit frequency shift from nonlinear interactions with the intense microwave field. Deterministic electron trapping at an intended position remains challenging due to solid neon surface roughness; we characterize the electron's position from its differential coupling to distinct electrodes. Although not trapped at an intended position, our estimates indicate that spin-qubit demonstrations remain feasible.

summary.summary: A single electron trapped on solid neon is coupled to a superconducting NbTiN nanowire resonator to realize a charge qubit with coherent microwave control at Rabi frequencies up to 76 MHz, an order of magnitude higher than previous work. The electron position is inferred from coupling strengths to multiple electrodes, and despite non-optimal trapping due to neon surface roughness, spin-qubit fidelities up to 99.995% are estimated to be achievable with integrated ferromagnets.
summary.motivation: Electrons on solid neon offer isolation from material defects and potentially long coherence times for quantum information processing, making them attractive for spin-qubit implementations that require magnetic-field-compatible resonators to deliver control signals.
summary.method: A single electron on solid neon was coupled to an NbTiN nanowire resonator (bare resonance $f_r = 5.345$ GHz, $Q_l = 1841$, $\kappa/2\pi = 2.9$ MHz) with coupling strength $g/2\pi = 2.1$ MHz determined by microwave spectroscopy; coherent control was demonstrated via Rabi oscillations, Ramsey interferometry, and Hahn-echo measurements.
summary.result: Rabi frequencies up to $f_{\mathrm{Rabi}} = 76$ MHz were achieved; charge-qubit coherence times $T_2^* = 91$ ns and $T_2 = 202$ ns were measured; energy relaxation $T_1 = 3.06$ μs was observed (improving to $17.7$ μs after annealing); spin-qubit gate fidelity estimated at $99.52\%$ using measured parameters or $99.995\%$ with post-annealing values and intermediate spin-relaxation rates.

papers.title: A Denser Planar Surface Code
papers.abstract: We present a quantum code implementable on a regular $2$D hex grid with an estimated encoding rate up to $4.5\times$ of that of a rotated surface code patch using circuit-level noise in a one- and two-qubit $10^{-3}$ error uniform depolarizing model. Our approach is based on yoking a dense packing of surface code twist defects, enabled by new stabilizer measurement cycles with an optimal four layers of nearest-neighbor two-qubit gates, almost no distance-reducing hook errors, and efficient decoding. We demonstrate a space-efficient architecture for computing on densely packed logical qubits, including new padding-free lattice surgery protocols in an optimal bounding box of $2d^2$ data and measurement qubits per patch. Assuming a $1μ$s surface code cycle time and a $10μ$s reaction time, these developments enable chemically accurate ground state phase estimation of a broad class of `utility-scale' electronic structure simulation problems such as the $108$ spin-orbital FeMoco-based nitrogen fixation catalyst in under a month with $89$k noisy superconducting qubits. We elucidate a Pareto frontier of space-time trade-offs and find a minimum physical quantum volume of $1.3$ mega-qubit-hours. These correspond to a $36\times$ space and $6.6\times$ spacetime improvement, respectively, over our previous state-of-the-art minimum-Toffoli resource estimates (Phys. Rev. X 15, 041016).

similar_to.title: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation

summary.summary: This work demonstrates a surface code implementation on a regular 2D hexagonal lattice achieving up to 4.5× the encoding rate of a rotated surface code patch by dense packing of twist defects with optimal 6-layer stabilizer measurement and no distance-reducing hook errors. Applied to chemically accurate ground state energy estimation of utility-scale molecules like the 108-spin-orbital FeMoco nitrogen fixation catalyst, the approach enables solution in under a month using only 89 k noisy qubits at $10^{-3}$ error rate, representing 36× space and 6.6× spacetime improvement over prior Toffoli-minimized designs.
summary.motivation: The surface code's low encoding rate of $2d^2 - 1$ physical qubits per logical qubit becomes a severe bottleneck for utility-scale quantum chemistry problems requiring 100+ spin-orbitals and code distances up to 27, necessitating millions of physical qubits. Twist defects theoretically enable higher rates but have been impractical due to heavy-weight stabilizers, circuit depth, or distance loss.
summary.method: The authors implement surface code twist defects on a degree-3 hex grid using subsystem measurement of lower-weight gauge operators in 6 optimal layers (4 CX + reset + measurement), enabling dense packings: 3-qubit rectangles at 1.5× rate, twist-defect grids at 2× asymptotic rate, and 1D yoked concatenation with $[[n,n-2,2]]$ parity checks at up to 4.5× rate. Extensive circuit-level noise benchmarks in the uniform $10^{-3}$ depolarizing model validate logical error scaling using Stim and sparse-blossom MWPM decoding.
summary.result: Memory error rate for Z-top patches: $p_\mathrm{dynamic}(d) = 10^{-1}(3.5^{-d/10})$; lattice surgery: $10^{-1}(3.5^{-d/30})$ per round. Three-qubit rectangles achieve empirical error matching single-qubit Z-top patches. Dense twist storage with parity check yoking exhibits logical error $\sim (n_\mathrm{row}^2/T_\mathrm{yoke})\,p_\mathrm{dynamic}^2(d)$ yielding effective distance $\sim 2d$ while reducing physical footprint from $3.2\times10^6$ qubits to $8.9\times10^4$ qubits for FeMoco-54 at 1 µs cycle time.

papers.title: Real-Time Quantum Error Correction System Stack: Architecture, Algorithms, and Engineering Practice
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is transitioning from physical feasibility demonstrations to systems engineering challenges. Google has achieved below-threshold performance on distance-5/7 surface codes, while Riverlane and Rigetti have demonstrated hardware-integrated low-latency feedback loops. These milestones indicate that the core challenge of real-time decoding has shifted from algorithmic capability to system-level engineering. However, a substantial engineering gap remains between laboratory demonstrations and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). This white paper addresses three questions: (1) Where are the real bottlenecks in real-time QEC: beyond average decoder speed, the constraints lie in QEC round time, tail latency, and end-to-end data path coordination; (2) How mature are mainstream decoder algorithms: we benchmark the major decoders for both surface codes and quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, evaluating their real-time readiness; (3) What system stack do we propose: a six-layer reference architecture from syndrome acquisition to logical operations, with interface definitions and latency budget models. Our results quantify the gap between current decoder performance and real-time requirements, and identify the architectural choices needed to close it.

similar_to.title: Demonstrating real-time and low-latency quantum error correction with superconducting qubits
Exponential suppression of bit or phase flip errors with repetitive error correction

summary.summary: This white paper analyzes real-time quantum error correction as a systems engineering problem, proposing a six-layer reference architecture from syndrome acquisition to logical operations and benchmarking major decoders (MWPM, Union-Find, BP+OSD, neural networks) across surface codes and qLDPC codes. The work quantifies the gap between current decoder performance and real-time requirements: MWPM meets the 1 μs per-round deadline for superconducting platforms only at $d \leq 7$ in batch mode, while window-mode decoding is 2–4× more expensive, and GPU-accelerated BP+OSD sustains <1 ms per round for $[\![288,12,18]\!]$ qLDPC codes.
summary.motivation: Quantum error correction has transitioned from algorithmic feasibility to systems engineering challenges following Google's below-threshold surface-code demonstrations, Riverlane/Rigetti's sub-microsecond integrated decoding, and Quantinuum's fault-tolerant logical operations, motivating a systematic analysis of the bottlenecks, latency budgets, and architectural requirements for scalable FTQC.
summary.method: The paper formalizes the end-to-end data path (stabilizer execution, readout, transport, decoding, feedforward), defines streaming versus synchronization regimes with distinct latency requirements, instantiates platform-specific constraints for superconducting ($\lambda \sim 1$ MHz), trapped-ion, and neutral-atom systems, benchmarks decoders under circuit-level depolarizing noise using Stim and PyMatching, and proposes a six-layer stack with heterogeneous compute dispatch, backlog management, and speculative decoding.
summary.result: Batch MWPM achieves $p_{99}$ <1 μs only at $d \leq 5$; window-mode MWPM exceeds 1 μs at all distances. GPU-accelerated BP+OSD for $[\![144,12,12]\!]$ qLDPC sustains 42.5 μs/round at $p=0.001$, meeting 1 ms targets for neutral atoms, while CPU BP+OSD hits 1.04 ms/round at the same code and noise. Speculative decoding, dynamic dispatch, and FPGA/GPU acceleration emerge as essential for scaling to $d \geq 17$ required by practical algorithms like RSA-2048 factoring (~$3.7 \times 10^9$ Toffoli gates).
